grammarSchedule.why: sein is taught in lesson 1 and haben in lesson 4, so 'Ich bin gut' is available immediately
gehen in lesson 1 already takes the regular endings on an unchanged stem (ich gehe, du gehst)
essen arrives in lesson 6 with Brot and Apfel: du isst, er isst
hier and dort in lesson 3 give the first element that can be fronted ahead of the verb
lesson 5 puts das Wasser, der Kaffee and die Milch side by side, the first three-gender contrast
die Eltern in lesson 11 is the first plural noun form; lesson 16 adds numbers to count Kinder with
trinken plus der Kaffee in lesson 5 gives the masculine der/den switch on a direct object
nicht is taught in lesson 2; kein arrives in lesson 24 with the articles it replaces
wie is in lesson 1 together with gehen and sein
mein arrives in lesson 9 with Haus, Zimmer and Tisch to agree with
wollen and trinken are both in lesson 5, so the infinitive can already be sent to the end
the same wollen plus trinken pair frames the first bracket; separable prefixes widen it from lesson 28
sich vorstellen and kennenlernen in lesson 28 are the first separable verbs; lesson 43 adds aufstehen, anfangen and the rest of the morning routine
bitte in lesson 2 with gehen from lesson 1 makes a du-imperative possible
mir, dir and ihm are taught in lesson 26, together with the geben and helfen that were already taught
mit and ohne in lesson 5 take Milch and Zucker; lesson 30 adds fuer, um, von, ab, aus and durch as a set
in is taught in lesson 4 but only lesson 9 supplies Haus and Zimmer to be in and to go into; an follows in lesson 77
lernen and kaufen give usable participles from lesson 7, but gestern in lesson 14 is the first point a Perfekt sentence reads as past
gehen and kommen are taught by lesson 13; gestern in lesson 14 makes 'Ich bin gestern gekommen' possible
anchored with the two Perfekt topics it serves; separable participles become showable in lesson 28 and plentiful in lesson 43
und in lesson 2 joins two clauses built from lesson 1; aber follows in 3, oder and denn in 8 and 42
nominative pronouns exist from lesson 1, but lesson 26 is the first place a pronoun can take an accusative or dative form
the course has no personal names; Berlin and Aachen in lesson 56 arrive next to Zentrum and Stadtplan, so 'Berlins Zentrum' is the first possible genitive
